newsitem.title: INDIA: Romanian, Gulf aircraft nearly collide over India.
newsitem.headline: Romanian, Gulf aircraft nearly collide over India.

text.p: Passenger planes with a total of nearly 370 people on board came close to colliding over India, months after 349 people died there in the world's worst mid-air crash, officials said on Tuesday.

A Tarom Romanian airline Airbus 310 and a Gulf Air Boeing 767 at the same altitude narrowly missed each other on Sunday, 44 nautical miles southwest of the Indian capital, P.C. Goyal, a senior official at the Airports Authority of India, told Reuters.
He said the two planes passed each other at a distance of nearly 500 feet (150 metres), less than half the standard distance for passage of 1,000 feet.
"There was a near-miss and it occurred on Sunday at around 11.30 a.m. (0600 GMT)," a Civil Aviation Ministry spokeswoman told Reuters.
"As per the prima facie evidence the air traffic controller was found at fault and he has been taken off duty," she said.
Goyal said the near-miss was due to human error.
"It was totally the air traffic controller's miscalculation...it was a pure and simple human error on the ground by the controller," he said.
The officials did not say how many passengers each aircraft was carrying. They said there were nearly 370 people on board in all.
The Press Trust of India said the Airbus, arriving from Bucharest, had been cleared for descent at 16,000 feet by air traffic control at New Delhi's international airport.
The Gulf Air aircraft on a flight to Dubai had ascended to the same level after taking off and the two planes approached each other at the same altitude, the news agency said.
Sophisticated airborne collision avoidance systems on the two aircraft helped avert a collision, the news agency said.
Last November a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter collided in mid-air near New Delhi, killing all 349 people aboard.

A special court of enquiry has yet to submit its report on the cause of the November collision. Since then, aviation officials say there have been 11 near-misses in Indian air space, most of them involving commercial airliners.
The collision has focused world attention on flight safety in India, where economic growth has spurred tourism, placing pressure on outdated air traffic systems.
A multi-million dollar plan to modernise radar and communications systems at major airports has fallen far behind schedule for technical reasons, officials say.
